nodes.referent: Robert Remak (1815-1865), German-Jewish physician, neurologist, and embryologist, born in Poznan/Posen (then Prussia) and working mainly in Berlin -- established that new animal cells arise through the division of pre-existing cells and worked out the differentiation of the three embryonic germ layers, and separately discovered unmyelinated nerve fibers ('fibers of Remak') and autonomic ganglia later named for him. Historically credited by some sources as the true originator of the 'cells only arise from pre-existing cells' tenet later published by Rudolf Virchow. NOT his grandson, the 20th-century mathematician Robert Remak (1888-1942) known for group-theory decomposition results, and not any other person sharing the surname.

nodes.rationale: Directly requested by the order and by the corpus's own reviewed data: the edge:rudolf-virchow-founded-cell-theory note explicitly names Remak as the next gap to close on concept:cell-theory. Remak is independently notable beyond this one priority question (embryology's germ-layer work, discovery of unmyelinated nerve fibers), so the node is warranted on ordinary compass grounds even apart from the contested edge proposed alongside it.

nodes.referent: Marcus Antonius von Plenciz (also written Marc Anton Plenciz or Plencic; c. 1705-1786), Austrian physician practicing in Vienna -- in his 1762 work Opera medico-physica proposed that each infectious disease is caused by its own specific, distinct kind of minute living organism ('contagium animatum'), an elaboration of Girolamo Fracastoro's earlier 1546 'seeds of disease' contagion theory, roughly a century before the germ theory of disease was experimentally confirmed by Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch. Not to be confused with any other bearer of the surname von Plenciz/Plenciz.

A dedicated biographical source on von Plenciz specifically has not been fetched this session [UNFETCHED] -- the name spelling, exact dates, and the 'Opera medico-physica' title above are from my own knowledge, not re-verified.

nodes.referent: William Whewell (1794-1866), English polymath, philosopher and historian of science, Master of Trinity College, Cambridge -- coined numerous scientific terms including 'scientist', 'physicist', 'uniformitarianism', and 'catastrophism' (the latter two introduced in his 1832 review of Charles Lyell's Principles of Geology, contrasting Lyell's gradualist position with the catastrophist view Whewell himself was more sympathetic to), and wrote History of the Inductive Sciences and Philosophy of the Inductive Sciences. Not to be confused with any other person named Whewell.

Full biographical sourcing, and the specific claim about the 1832 review and Whewell's own catastrophist sympathies, have not been fetched this session [UNFETCHED] -- from my own knowledge.

The claim that Whewell personally favored catastrophism over Lyell's uniformitarianism is from my own knowledge, not verified this session, and if wrong would undercut part of the referent description (though not his authorship of the term itself, which the corpus's own already-reviewed note already establishes).
